Chapter Two: The Journey of Racial Identity in Childhood and Adolescence
As kids move from those early years into elementary school, their world starts to open up—and suddenly, everything feels a bit more complicated, doesn’t it? Friendships shift, new groups form, and the differences that were once simple now carry so much more meaning. For many Black children and other kids of color, figuring out who they are in relation to race becomes a huge part of growing up.
Think about it: in those first few grades, most kids just want to fit in. They notice who gets invited to birthday parties, who’s picked first for games, and who always sits together at lunch. Sometimes, a child with darker skin or a different accent finds themselves left out—not because of something they’ve done, but simply because of how others see them. The sting of being excluded can be subtle—a joke, a look, maybe a teacher who doesn’t expect as much from them—but even small moments like these can leave a lasting mark.
By the time middle school rolls around, the pressure to belong is even stronger. Adolescents are searching for who they are, and race becomes one of the ways they define themselves. For Black students, this journey often means facing stereotypes and assumptions from others. Imagine a boy who loves science being told he’s “acting white,” or a girl who’s outspoken in class getting labeled as “loud.” And it isn’t just their classmates—sometimes these messages come from teachers, counselors, even family members.
In one school, a group of Black students started sitting together in the cafeteria. To people watching from the outside, it might’ve looked like they were separating themselves. But honestly, for those at that table, it was a safe haven. It was a space to relax, laugh, and share stories—no need to explain themselves or worry about being misunderstood. That table became a spot to process the daily slights and mix-ups that came with being one of the only Black students in a mostly white school. It wasn’t about shutting others out. It was about finally having a place to just be themselves.
You’ll see this pattern in schools all over the country. Students of color often group together—not because they’re being unfriendly, but because they need affirmation and understanding. When you ask them why, many will say it’s the one place where they don’t have to worry about being judged for their culture, language, or how they look. And here’s something interesting: for white students, who rarely have to think about their own racial identity, these groups can seem confusing or even threatening. They might not realize their own friendships are just as homogenous, but go unnoticed—because whiteness is often seen as the default.
The journey of racial identity is different for everyone. Some kids of color try to blend in, hoping to be accepted by downplaying what makes them different. Others lean into their heritage, joining cultural clubs or going to community events. Family, community, and the messages they hear from the world all shape how this unfolds. Sometimes, a single moment—a teacher’s comment, a story on the news, or a friend’s betrayal—can kick off a period of deep self-reflection.
And white students? They’re on their own journey, too, even if it isn’t talked about as much. Many grow up in places where race just isn’t discussed, and their own identity is taken for granted. When they finally come face to face with privilege and bias, some feel defensive or even guilty, unsure what to do next. Others start to question the stories they’ve heard, searching for new ways to understand themselves and the people around them.
Adolescence is a time of searching, and race is just one piece of the puzzle every young person is trying to put together. The cafeteria table is just one example of how students navigate these waters, looking for places where they feel seen and understood. Ultimately, the real challenge isn’t about forcing everyone to mix together. It’s about building environments where every student feels safe to explore who they are—without fear, and without shame.
